small_step_desc: In this small step, students practise calculating the mean, median and mode from ungrouped frequency tables. Students have already covered calculating the mean from a frequency table in Year 8, but this may be their first time calculating the mode and median. Begin by helping students interpret the table, identifying the values and their frequencies. For the mean, guide them to multiply each value by its frequency, total these products and divide by the overall number of data points. When finding the mode, prompt students to identify the most frequent value. For the median, guide students to explore the cumulative frequency and find the middle value either through a cumulative frequency column or an ordered list.

small_step: Mean from a grouped frequency table
small_step_name: Mean from a grouped frequency table
small_step_desc: In this small step, students estimate the mean from grouped frequency tables. This may have previously been covered in Year 8 as an extend step. Begin by reviewing how to calculate the mean from raw data to highlight the difference when working with grouped data. Emphasise that when data is grouped, individual values are unknown, so the mean can only be estimated. Explain that the midpoint of each interval is used as a representative value, assuming an even distribution within each group. Model the process step by step, showing how to identify midpoints, multiply them by their corresponding frequencies, sum these products, and divide by the total frequency to find an estimated mean.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of data collection by exploring sampling, a method used to gather information from part of a population when it isn’t practical to survey everyone. Begin by defining the population as the entire group being studied, such as all students in a school, and a sample as a smaller group representing it. Introduce random sampling, where each individual has an equal chance of being selected, and systematic sampling, where selections are made at regular intervals. Once students are confident, explore stratified sampling, where the population is divided into groups (strata) and a proportional sample is taken from each. Encourage students to apply proportional reasoning to calculate sample sizes and discuss which method is most reliable in different situations. Emphasise the importance of avoiding bias when selecting samples.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students use proportional reasoning to estimate a population with the capture–recapture method. Using familiar examples, such as estimating the number of fish in a pond, helps make the idea relatable and emphasises why estimation is needed when counting every individual is impractical. Begin by discussing the key assumption that the proportion of marked individuals in the second sample reflects the proportion in the entire population. For instance, if 10 fish are marked initially and, in a second sample of 20 fish, 2 are marked, then 10 N = 2 20 . Have students solve to calculate N to see how the population estimate arises from proportional reasoning. Conclude by discussing when estimates may be unreliable, such as when marked fish don’t mix evenly, highlighting the importance of the method’s assumptions.

Begin by exploring examples where the roots and y-intercept can be identified through inspection before introducing algebraic methods. Emphasise that the roots of the equation y = ax2 + bx + c correspond to the solutions of ax2 + bx + c = 0 and should be written in the form x = d. Remind students that the y-intercept can be found by substituting x = 0 into the equation to identify the value of y before writing as a coordinate in the form (0, y). Provide opportunities for students to explore graphs that have 0, 1 or 2 roots, helping them recognise how the number of solutions relates to the graph’s intersection with the x-axis. Dynamic graphing software can be used to support understanding.

Begin by exploring examples where the roots and y-intercept can be identified through inspection before introducing algebraic methods. Emphasise that the roots of the equation y = ax2 + bx + c correspond to the solutions of ax2 + bx + c = 0 and should be written in the form x = d. Remind students that the y-intercept can be found by substituting x = 0 into the equation to identify the value of y before writing as a coordinate in the form (0, y). Provide opportunities for students to explore graphs that have 0, 1 or 2 roots, helping them recognise how the number of solutions relates to the graph’s intersection with the x-axis. Dynamic graphing software can be used to support understanding.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students estimate the mean from grouped frequency tables. This may have previously been covered in Year 8 as an extend step. Begin by reviewing how to calculate the mean from raw data to highlight the difference when working with grouped data. Emphasise that when data is grouped, individual values are unknown, so the mean can only be estimated. Explain that the midpoint of each interval is used as a representative value, assuming an even distribution within each group. Model the process step by step, showing how to identify midpoints, multiply them by their corresponding frequencies, sum these products, and divide by the total frequency to find an estimated mean.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students identify the median and modal class for grouped data, and estimate the mean. This could be combined with the previous step. Begin by helping students rewrite the data from the frequency table as a list to strengthen their understanding of the median. Highlight the link between finding the median in a list and locating it in the table before introducing the use of cumulative frequency. Model how to calculate the median position using n + 1 2 , and guide students in creating a cumulative frequency column to identify the class interval containing the median. Emphasise that the median is an estimate representing a range of values rather than an exact value. For the modal class, prompt students to identify the class interval with the highest frequency, explaining that this represents the most common range of values, not a single mode.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students plot additional lines on graphs to find solutions to equations, building on their understanding of finding roots of quadratics from graphs. This step reinforces the equivalence of roots and solutions of equations in the form ax2 + bx + c = 0 Start by asking them to draw a given horizontal line in the form y = d alongside a graph of the form y = ax2 + bx + c to solve ax2 + bx + c = d. For example, the solutions of the equation x2 + 5x + 6 = 1 can be found by identifying the x-coordinates of the points where the graphs y = x2 + 5x + 6 and y = 1 intersect. Once students are confident, introduce further examples requiring lines of the form y = ax + b, supporting students to determine and plot the correct additional line. Emphasise the importance of avoiding bias when selecting samples.

Encourage students to calculate the gradient of the radius first, then use this to determine the gradient of the tangent. Model how the gradient and the coordinates of the given point form the equation of the tangent in the form y = mx + c

Highlight that they form a straight line and therefore sum to 180°. Remind students that the sum of interior angles can be calculated using (n – 2) × 180°, where n is the number of sides, and that this can also be used to work out the number of sides when the sum of interior angles is known. small_step_desc: In this extend step, students begin to use clear reasoning to prove geometric facts. Start by revisiting familiar angle facts, ensuring students can state each fact accurately. Model how to build a simple chain of reasoning using statements such as “because alternate angles are equal” or “because angles in a triangle sum to 180°”. Encourage students to write each step clearly and to justify their answers. Make sure that students understand that a proof must show a fact works in every case, not just for one example. Model to students how to structure their reasoning so it clearly shows a logical progression from the given information to the conclusion. Provide opportunities to spot errors in worked examples so they can recognise incomplete or incorrect reasoning. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not justify their answers or give reasons for why they have applied certain angle facts. • Students may write conclusions without clearly showing the logical steps that lead to them. • Students may assume that diagrams are drawn to scale when they are not. • Students may believe they have proven a fact when they have only shown it works for one case. small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap prior learning from Key Stage 3 that the angles in a triangle sum to 180°. Encourage students to describe what is the same and what is different between examples, such as comparing angles in an isosceles and an equilateral triangle. Ensure students are confident using three-letter notation when identifying and labelling angles. Provide examples where students apply more than one angle fact, such as when finding unknown angles in triangles within larger diagrams. Emphasise that time is always plotted on the horizontal axis and that equal intervals are essential. Encourage students to discuss upward or downward trends, along with periods of stability. Emphasise that while time series graphs highlight overall trends, short-term fluctuations may not always reflect the longer-term trend. small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap prior learning that the interior angles of a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Begin by highlighting the connection to the sum of angles in a triangle, showing how any quadrilateral can be divided into two triangles and hence, the angles in a quadrilateral sum to 360°. Use a range of examples, including rectangles, parallelograms, trapezia, and kites, to reinforce that the total is always 360°. Encourage students to provide reasons alongside their answers, and to label angles accurately using three-letter notation. Provide examples where they need to apply more than one angle fact, such as combining the sum of angles in a quadrilateral with angles on a straight line. Emphasise clear reasoning and checking that answers are sensible. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that the angles in a quadrilateral sum to 180° rather than 360°. • Students may assume a quadrilateral cannot include an interior reflex angle. • Students may assume that opposite angles in any quadrilateral are always equal. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 1 – Angles | Step 3 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about the sum of angles in a triangle and angles in a quadrilateral? • Do quadrilaterals always contain right angles? Explain how you know. • How can you use the sum of angles in a triangle to work out the sum of the angles in a quadrilateral? • Can a quadrilateral have three obtuse angles? Why or why not? • If one angle in a quadrilateral is increased, what happens to the sum of the rest of the angles? Explain how you know. • A quadrilateral contains angles of 60°, 85° and 100°. What is the size of the fourth angle? Explain how you know. small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap their prior learning of interior and exterior angles from Key Stage 3. Remind them that the sum of the exterior angles of any polygon is 360° and use this to calculate individual exterior angles in regular polygons by dividing 360° by the number of sides. Highlight that interior and exterior angles sum to 180°, and use this to calculate unknown exterior angles given an interior angle. Students can then extend this knowledge to find the number of sides of a regular polygon when either the interior or exterior angle is known. Encourage students to clearly label diagrams to support reasoning, and to help identify when sides or angles are equal. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe that the exterior and interior angles sum to 360°. • Students may believe that the sum of exterior angles depends on the number of sides the polygon has. • Students may assume that some equal angles always mean the polygon is regular, without checking that all sides are also equal in length. small_step_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret stem-and-leaf diagrams. Begin by explaining that these diagrams organise numerical data, using the stem to show place value and the leaf to show the final digit, allowing all values to remain visible. Emphasise that including a clear key is essential so the data can be correctly interpreted. Model how to organise the data, select a suitable stem, and record each leaf clearly so digits align. Revisit how to calculate averages and the range by finding the difference between the greatest and smallest values in the set. Include examples with decimal values, such as 7|3 representing 7.3 As students develop confidence, introduce back-to-back stem- and-leaf diagrams to compare two data sets. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may write leaves out of order instead of listing them from smallest to largest. • Students may forget to include a key, which can make it difficult to interpret the values represented. small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning of interior angles of polygons from Key Stage 3. Begin by revisiting the relationship between interior and exterior angles. Highlight that they form a straight line and therefore sum to 180°. Remind students that the sum of interior angles can be calculated using (n – 2) × 180°, where n is the number of sides, and that this can also be used to work out the number of sides when the sum of interior angles is known. It can be useful to model splitting polygons into triangles to demonstrate why this method works to calculate the sum of interior angles. Reinforce that “regular” means that all sides and angles are equal. Calculators may be used throughout this step, so the focus remains on the method rather than the arithmetic. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse interior and exterior angles. • Students may believe that the interior angle sum is the same for all polygons. • Students may believe the interior angle sum is found by multiplying the number of sides by 180°. • Students may believe that all interior angles are equal in size even when the polygon is irregular. small_step_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of drawing histograms to now interpret them. Recap that histograms show continuous data and that the area of each bar represents frequency. Guide students to examine a single bar and identify what they know, such as the class boundaries and the height. Ask students how these two features could be used to calculate the frequency. Support students to derive the relationship, frequency = frequency density × class width. Provide opportunities to estimate values within an interval, including estimating a value for the median by accumulating frequencies. Encourage students to express parts of the distribution as fractions and percentages once they have calculated the total frequency. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may believe the frequency is represented by the height of the bar rather than the area. • Students may use class midpoints rather than class boundaries when estimating values. small_step_desc: In this small step, students explore how cumulative frequency diagrams are constructed from grouped data. small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of cumulative frequency diagrams by interpreting the data shown. Remind students that each plotted point represents a cumulative total. Guide students to identify an estimate for the median and lower and upper quartiles by finding 25%, 50% and 75% of the total frequency and locating these values on the curve. Students then calculate the interquartile range by subtracting the lower quartile from the upper quartile. They should also be able to compare two cumulative frequency diagrams by considering the median and interquartile range and deduce what these comparisons indicate. Encourage accurate reading of values by drawing horizontal and vertical lines and discuss why this method is more reliable than estimating by eye. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may attempt to find quartiles using the horizontal axis instead of the cumulative frequency axis. • Students may read values directly from the curve without drawing horizontal and vertical lines, resulting in inaccuracies. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 8 Mathematical talk • What does each plotted point represent on a cumulative frequency diagram? • How do we know where to find 25%, 50% and 75% of the data? • Why are the values for the median, upper and lower quartiles only an estimate? • What does the interquartile range tell us about the distribution of the data? • What does the graph tell us about the value below which 10% of the data lies? • Why can’t the range be identified from a grouped frequency table or a cumulative frequency table? Encourage students to write each step clearly and to justify their answers. Make sure that students understand that a proof must show a fact works in every case, not just for one example. Model to students how to structure their reasoning so it clearly shows a logical progression from the given information to the conclusion. Provide opportunities to spot errors in worked examples so they can recognise incomplete or incorrect reasoning. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not justify their answers or give reasons for why they have applied certain angle facts. • Students may write conclusions without clearly showing the logical steps that lead to them. • Students may assume that diagrams are drawn to scale when they are not. • Students may believe they have proven a fact when they have only shown it works for one case. small_step_desc: In this small step, students learn how to represent the distribution of data sets by drawing box plots. Highlight that a box plot is formed from 5 values from a given data set: the median, the upper and lower quartiles and the minimum and maximum values. Use of a visualiser is recommended when modelling how to draw a box plot. Students can also explore the relationships between data represented on a cumulative frequency diagram and a box plot and identify quartiles carefully before drawing a box plot. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misinterpret scales when drawing box plots. • Students may not recognise that they need to calculate missing values needed to draw a box plot. For example, if they are given the range and the lowest value, they need to work out the maximum value. small_step_desc: In this small step, students build on their prior learning of pictograms from Year 8. Begin by revisiting how discrete data is represented and how each symbol, or part of a symbol, corresponds to a value shown in the key. Highlight the importance of using the key carefully, both when constructing pictograms and when interpreting them. Once students are confident with this skill, support them in finishing partially completed pictograms by checking that the frequencies are shown correctly. Students should also practise interpreting pictograms by explaining what the data represents and making comparisons between categories where relevant. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may draw a pictogram without a key. • Students may choose a symbol for their key that makes it hard to represent part values. • Students may disregard the key and assume each symbol always represents one item. • Students may treat part symbols as whole symbols, leading to incorrect frequencies. alignment_justification: The video effectively focuses on interpreting pictograms, aligning well with the target objective of understanding how symbols represent data and the importance of the key. It addresses key concepts like calculating values from symbols and comparing data, which are essential for learners new to the topic. However, it could improve by explicitly discussing common misconceptions and errors related to pictograms.
instruction_justification: The transcript provides a clear explanation of pictograms, focusing on the key concept of how symbols represent data. It includes worked examples and student engagement prompts, which help reinforce understanding. However, some terms could be simplified further, and the introduction of new terms could be better defined to enhance clarity for learners new to the topic.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students build on their prior learning of pictograms from Year 8. Begin by revisiting how discrete data is represented and how each symbol, or part of a symbol, corresponds to a value shown in the key. Highlight the importance of using the key carefully, both when constructing pictograms and when interpreting them. Once students are confident with this skill, support them in finishing partially completed pictograms by checking that the frequencies are shown correctly. Students should also practise interpreting pictograms by explaining what the data represents and making comparisons between categories where relevant. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may draw a pictogram without a key. • Students may choose a symbol for their key that makes it hard to represent part values. • Students may disregard the key and assume each symbol always represents one item. • Students may treat part symbols as whole symbols, leading to incorrect frequencies. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 1 Mathematical talk • What does the key in this pictogram tell us? • What mistake might someone make if they ignore the key? • What symbol could be used to represent the key? • How do you know how many symbols to draw? • How could you represent a frequency that is not a multiple of the key value? • What value is represented by a half, a quarter or three quarters of a symbol? • How would the pictogram change if the value of the key was doubled or halved? • Do the symbols need to be the same size? Why or why not? small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of vectors beyond the context of translating shapes, which they previously encountered in Year 9. This step will focus on interpreting column vectors and representing vectors as diagrams. Remind students that the top number in a column vector represents the horizontal direction, while the bottom number represents the vertical direction. It is important that students understand that a vector shows both direction and magnitude. The role of the arrow should also be emphasised, as it indicates the start point, end point, and direction of the vector. Comparing similar vectors can help to reinforce this understanding, for example by comparing 3 4 -   and -3 4   . Misconceptions and common errors • Students may neglect to draw arrows on vectors. • Students may draw arrows in the wrong direction on vectors. • Students may misinterpret column vectors, such as reading 2 4 -   as ‘2 up and 4 left’ rather than ‘2 right and 4 down’. small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap their Year 8 learning on constructing and interpreting vertical line charts and bar charts. Remind students that vertical line charts represent discrete data using lines drawn against various categories, with the height showing the frequency, while bar charts use rectangular bars to show the same information. Highlight that both charts use clearly labelled axes and consistent, equally spaced scales, with equal spacing between each line or bar. It can be helpful to compare a vertical line chart with a bar chart representing the same data to highlight the similarities in data presentation. As confidence develops, encourage students to compare frequencies and calculate the mode, range and mean from the charts. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may place numbers on the y-axis in unequal intervals resulting in a distorted scale. • Students may place vertical lines or bars at irregular gaps along the horizontal axis, rather than spacing them evenly. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 2 Mathematical talk • How do you know which axis shows the categories and which shows the frequency? • How can you describe the scale being used? • Do the lines or bars need an equal gap between them? Explain your answer. • How do you know what frequency each vertical line or bar represents? • What is the same and what is different about a vertical line chart and a bar chart? • If the scale goes up in 2s, where would you plot a frequency of 5? • How would this data look if it was shown in a different orientation? small_step_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of vector representations as column vectors and directed line segments by introducing notation for labelling vectors. Different conventions should be introduced, such as writing a vector as AB , emphasising that this represents the vector from A to B. Students should also be given opportunities to work with vectors labelled using bold letters, such as a or x. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may misinterpret vectors, for example reading XY as YX . • Students may neglect to draw arrows on the vectors or draw arrows in the wrong direction. • Students may neglect to label vectors. For example, not labelling ‘E’ and ‘F’ on either end of a line segment to represent the vector EF . small_step_desc: In this small step, students explore vectors that are parallel to each other. Introduce students to the concept of a scalar, emphasising that it is the value by which a vector is multiplied. Students should recognise that when one vector is a scalar multiple of another, the two vectors are parallel. Begin by using diagrams to represent different vectors, for example by comparing a and 2a on a grid, highlighting that both are parallel and that 2a is twice the magnitude of a. This can then be used to build towards multiplying column vectors by a scalar. Emphasise that both the horizontal and vertical components of a column vector are multiplied by the scalar. Students should also have opportunities to explore the effect of multiplying vectors by negative scalars; for example, multiplying by –1 reverses the direction of a vector. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly when calculating with negative numbers. • Students may neglect to multiply both values in a column vector by the scalar. small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap their learning of drawing pie charts from Year 8. As students increase in confidence, provide them with data in other formats such as percentages, fractions or data displayed in bar charts. Highlight that this means a parallelogram has two pairs of identical vectors. Draw students’ attention to the direction of arrows on diagrams and how this can affect the result of a vector journey and the accurate evaluation of vector addition or subtraction. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may neglect the direction of arrows on a vector diagram, such as using the vector a rather than –a. • Students may not recognise properties leading to vectors which aren’t labelled on diagrams. For example, using the fact that opposite sides in a parallelogram are parallel and equal in length. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 3 – Vectors | Step 7 Mathematical talk • Which quadrilaterals have pairs of parallel sides? small_step_desc: In this small step, students draw and interpret stem-and-leaf diagrams. Begin by explaining that these diagrams organise numerical data, using the stem to show place value and the leaf to show the final digit, allowing all values to remain visible. Emphasise that including a clear key is essential so the data can be correctly interpreted. Model how to organise the data, select a suitable stem, and record each leaf clearly so digits align. Revisit how to calculate averages and the range by finding the difference between the greatest and smallest values in the set. Include examples with decimal values, such as 7|3 representing 7.3 As students develop confidence, introduce back-to-back stem- and-leaf diagrams to compare two data sets. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may write leaves out of order instead of listing them from smallest to largest. • Students may forget to include a key, which can make it difficult to interpret the values represented. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 2 – Graphs and diagrams | Step 8 Mathematical talk • What does the stem represent in this diagram? How do you know? • Why do we list the leaves in ascending order rather than the order they were collected? • Why is a key important when interpreting the values from a stem-and-leaf diagram? • What is the smallest value and what is the largest? How do you know? • What does the length of each row suggest about the distribution of values? • How would this diagram change if the data included decimals? • When might a back-to-back stem-and-leaf diagram be useful? small_step_desc: In this small step, students explore parallel vectors, recognising that vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other. Students may have some understanding of this concept from earlier steps in this block. Highlight that parallel vectors have the same (or opposite) direction but may differ in magnitude. Support strategies for proving that column vectors are parallel by using vectors represented on grids to emphasise the link between vectors and scalars. After this, model how to prove that algebraic vectors are parallel through factorisation. Once students are confident, move on to more complex problems where they may need to consider vector journeys to compare two vectors. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may think vectors are parallel if they have the same magnitude. • Students may not recognise parallel vectors involving negative scalars. For example, writing 6 2 -   as –2 × -3 1   to show 6 2 -   and -3 1   are parallel. • Students may find it difficult to write algebraic expressions for vectors that represent movement in the opposite direction. small_step_desc: In this small step, students recap finding the highest common factor (HCF), lowest common multiple (LCM), and writing numbers as a product of prime factors from Key Stage 3. Use practical contexts to reinforce when HCF or LCM is needed, and model listing with small numbers to show why it becomes inefficient for greater values. Revisit prime factorisation using factor trees, emphasising that every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation. Use Venn diagrams to organise information, highlighting that the HCF is the product of the common factors, while the LCM is the product of all factors within the diagram. Link back to listing to show both methods give the same result. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may include non-prime factors in their final product. • Students may confuse factors and multiples, particularly when using listing methods. • Students may rely on listing methods for large numbers, leading to inefficiency and increased likelihood of error. • Students may multiply all prime factors when finding the HCF, rather than only those common to all numbers. small_step_desc: In this small step, students explore vectors that are parallel to each other. Introduce students to the concept of a scalar, emphasising that it is the value by which a vector is multiplied. Students should recognise that when one vector is a scalar multiple of another, the two vectors are parallel. Begin by using diagrams to represent different vectors, for example by comparing a and 2a on a grid, highlighting that both are parallel and that 2a is twice the magnitude of a. This can then be used to build towards multiplying column vectors by a scalar. Emphasise that both the horizontal and vertical components of a column vector are multiplied by the scalar. Students should also have opportunities to explore the effect of multiplying vectors by negative scalars; for example, multiplying by –1 reverses the direction of a vector. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may make arithmetic errors, particularly when calculating with negative numbers. • Students may neglect to multiply both values in a column vector by the scalar. Explain how you know. • How do we know if one vector is a multiple of the other? • What is a scalar? • What is the effect of multiplying a vector by a negative scalar? • How does multiplying a vector by a scalar change its magnitude? small_step_desc: In this small step, students explore fractional indices. Some students may have previously covered this as an extend step in Year 8. Ensure students are fluent with square roots, cube roots and higher roots before introducing fractional indices using numerical bases. Develop understanding by reasoning from index laws, for example 9 1 2 × 9 1 2 = 91, and link this to 9 = 3 since 3 × 3 = 9. Use this to generalise that the denominator of a fractional index indicates the root. Once students are confident with unit fractional indices, introduce non-unit fractional indices, emphasising that the numerator represents a power applied after the root. Extend to fractional bases and negative fractional indices by linking back to negative indices as reciprocals. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the roles of the numerator and denominator, for example interpreting 64 3 2 as a cube root squared instead of a square root cubed. • Students may attempt to calculate a fraction of the base rather than taking the root and then applying the power. small_step_desc: In this small step, students learn how to add column vectors. Remind students that a vector has a horizontal component and a vertical component and that these components can be represented as column vectors. Emphasise that when adding two vectors, the resultant vector is found by adding the horizontal components together and the vertical components together. As with previous steps, visual representations of addition of vectors can help students to build a deeper understanding. Provide opportunities to draw vector diagrams to show how one vector follows another, making the connection between the geometric path and the numerical calculation. Once learning is secure move on to more abstract calculations, such as adding two column vectors. small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of surds by exploring how the number inside a square root affects how it can be simplified. Model how to simplify surds by rewriting the number inside the root as a product including a square factor, for example 18 = 9 × 2. Emphasise the importance of identifying a square factor as the result of square rooting a square number will be an integer. Highlight that it is often efficient to identify the greatest square factor to simplify a surd. If students cannot spot a square factor encourage the use of a factor tree to show the prime factorisation, for example 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 . Emphasise that this method relies on pairing equal factors to form a square number that can be square rooted. Once students are confident, extend this to other contexts such as area calculations or simplifying algebraic expressions. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may not fully simplify a surd, leaving a square factor inside the square root when more than one square factor is present. For example, 72 = 4 x 18 = 2 18 • Students may try to partition a surd using addition or subtraction, for example writing 18 = 9 + 9 Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 5 Mathematical talk • Why does writing the number inside the square root as a product help us simplify a surd? • What does it mean for a surd to be fully simplified? • Which factor pair includes the greatest square factor? • How does a prime factor tree help us identify square factors? • How can we check that a surd cannot be simplified any further? • Why must we identify a square factor when simplifying a surd? • What happens if we try to take out a factor that is not a square number? • What are the factor pairs of ? • What are the prime factors of ? small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop their understanding of surds by expanding and simplifying single brackets, such as a(b + c) and a( b + c). Once students are confident, they could be introduced to expanding and simplifying expressions involving two single brackets. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may try to combine surds and integers, for example 2 + 3 = 5 • Students may assume a × a æ a rather than a. • Students may not simplify surds fully after expansion, for example writing 2 + 12 rather than 2 + 2 3. small_step_desc: In this small step, students rationalise denominators that contain a single surd, building on their understanding of surds and rational numbers. Model the process by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same surd so that the denominator becomes a rational number. For example, when the denominator is 2, multiply both the numerator and denominator by 2 so the denominator becomes 2. Emphasise that the value of the fraction does not change, only its form. Remind students to simplify the resulting fraction fully, including simplifying surds by considering square factors where possible. Keep the focus on single-term denominators such as 3 or 3 5. Rationalising denominators containing binomials will be covered later in the block. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may multiply only the denominator by the surd instead of multiplying both the numerator and denominator. • Students may think the value of the fraction changes when rationalising the denominator, rather than staying equivalent. • Students may not simplify fully after rationalising, including simplifying any surds or cancelling common factors. small_step_desc: In this small step, students extend their understanding of expanding single brackets with surds to expanding and simplifying double brackets. Model expansion by multiplying each term in the first bracket by each term in the second bracket, making all four products explicit. Area or grid models can help students see the structure and avoid missing terms. When simplifying after expansion, remind students that only like surds can be combined, and that surds may need further simplification by taking out square factors. This may lead to integer results or simpler surd forms. Once students are confident, they can be challenged with more complex expressions in the form (a + b c)(d + e c). Misconceptions and common errors • Students may only multiply the first and last terms in each brackets, for example writing ( 2 + 3)( 2 + 5) = 2 + 15 = 17 • Students may incorrectly simplify expressions, for example 10 + 5 2 + 2 + 2 = 19 • Students may not simplify products of surds where possible after expansion or may not realise it is possible for the final answer to be an integer. Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 8 Mathematical talk • What is the same and what is different about expanding (x + 2)(x + 5) and ( x + 2)( x + 5)? • When we multiply two surds, what happens to the numbers inside the square root? Explain your answer. • Explain why 3 × 3 = 9 can be simplified, but 2 × 5 = 10 cannot be simplified further. • What do you notice when (a + b)(a – b) is expanded and simplified? Why do the surd terms cancel when simplifying? • What is the difference between simplifying a × a and simplifying a + a? • Can any of the surds in the resulting expansion be simplified further? Why or why not? small_step_desc: In this extend step, students will rationalise denominators with binomial expressions e.g. 1 + 5 2 Draw attention to the structure (a + b)(a – b), and highlight that this is a difference of two squares, simplifying to a2 – b, where the result will be an integer. Students will use this understanding to rationalise the denominator of a fraction, by multiplying both the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator. Emphasise that this is equivalent to multiplying by 1, so the value of the fraction does not change. Begin with examples such as 1 5 2 – where the denominator can be simplified to a positive integer, before moving on to more complex fractions such as 3 1 5 – where the denominator simplifies to a negative integer or 1 3 7 3 + + where the numerator has two terms. small_step_desc: In this small step, students build on their Key Stage 3 understanding of prime numbers and factors to write a number as a product of its prime factors. It can be helpful to begin with integers that have two or three prime factors before increasing complexity and introducing index notation. Encourage students to use a prime factor tree to organise information and identify prime factors. Ensure students understand that the product of the prime factors is equivalent to the original number. Emphasise that every integer greater than 1 has a unique prime factorisation, and that the order of the factors does not matter. As confidence increases, encourage students to make connections between the prime factor decomposition of related numbers. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may include non-prime factors in their final product. • Students may not work systematically, leading to missing or repeated factors. • Students may list prime factors, rather than writing them as a product. small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop their learning from Key Stage 3 by finding the highest common factor (HCF) and lowest common multiple (LCM) of two or more numbers. Although both concepts are introduced in Key Stage 3, ensure the difference between them is made explicit and that students practise examples of each separately. Link HCF to sharing and grouping, and LCM to repeating patterns or cycles. It may be useful to use the same pair of numbers to find both the HCF and the LCM and compare how the methods and final answers differ. Once students are confident, they can progress to using Venn diagrams to calculate the HCF and LCM. When using Venn diagrams, model the process using prime factorisation and encourage students to check that their answer makes sense in context. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse the HCF and LCM, especially when answering questions in context. • Students may assume the LCM of two numbers is always their product. • Students may place prime factors incorrectly in a Venn diagram, including duplicating factors, which leads to an incorrect HCF or LCM. small_step_desc: In this small step, students develop fluency with square and cube numbers and their corresponding roots. Begin by modelling square numbers using concrete manipulatives, such as counters arranged in a square, before linking this to area models and the calculation of a number multiplied by itself. Model cube numbers using concrete volume representations, such as interlocking cubes, to demonstrate multiplying a number by itself twice, before moving to more abstract representations. Show how cube numbers can be generated from square numbers by multiplying by the original number. Encourage students to be familiar with the first 15 square numbers and at least the first five cube numbers to support later work with square and cube roots. Emphasise that square and cube roots are the inverse operations of squaring and cubing. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may confuse square and cube numbers. • Students may divide a number by 2 to calculate its square root or by 3 to calculate its cube root. • Students may believe that all square roots and cube roots are integers. Model using a calculator to evaluate powers and roots, including brackets with negative numbers. Use patterns to explore powers of negative numbers, focusing on how the sign changes with even and odd powers. Introduce zero powers through sequences such as 23, 22, 21, discussing why 20 = 1 Support estimation of square and higher roots by locating values between known powers and using this to check answers are sensible. small_step_desc: In this extend step, students simplify expressions with surds by multiplying by surds, multiplying by integers, and adding or subtracting like surds. Emphasise that surds behave like algebraic terms and that simplifying means rewriting an expression in an equivalent, simpler form. Model multiplying surds by multiplying the values inside the roots, for example 7 × 3 = 21. Show that multiplying by an integer, for example 2 × 5 represents “2 lots of 5” which is equivalent to 2 5 Highlight that some products simplify to an integer, such as 4 × 4 = 16 = 4, so students should check whether further simplification is possible. When adding and subtracting, reinforce that only like surds can be combined, for example 3 2 + 5 2 = 8 2, but 2 + 3 cannot be simplified. Misconceptions and common errors • Students may try to add or subtract surds with different bases, for example 2 + 3 • Students may multiply integers and surds incorrectly, for example writing 2 × 5 = 10 • Students may not recognise when the product of surds simplifies to an integer, such as 4 × 4 = 4 Year 10 | Summer term | Block 4 – Factors, powers and surds | Step 8 Mathematical talk • When we multiply two surds, what happens to the numbers inside the square roots? • Why does 2 × 3 become 6, but not simplify further? • Why does 4 × 4 become 16? Why can this be simplified to 4? • What stays the same and what changes when we multiply a surd by an integer? Explain how you know. • Can all surds be simplified by addition and subtraction? Why or why not? • How is adding and subtracting surds similar to collecting like terms in algebra? • How can we check that an expression involving surds is fully simplified? Emphasise that the locus of points a fixed distance from a point forms a circle and discuss how the wording of a question determines whether it refers to points inside, on, or outside the circle. Students also investigate the locus of points a fixed distance from a line, and can extend this concept by constructing loci around other shapes, such as squares.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students enlarge shapes using positive integer scale factors, building on their understanding of similarity. Start with enlargements on a grid and highlight that scale factors greater than 1 produce larger images. As students progress, introduce enlargements with a given centre of enlargement. Encourage students to count distances from the centre of enlargement to each vertex of the shape and multiply it by the scale factor to determine the corresponding vertices of the image. Provide practice using centres that are not at the origin. Students should also work out the scale factor of an enlargement, and identify the centre of enlargement by drawing ray lines through the corresponding vertices of the object and image. The point where the ray lines meet is the centre of enlargement. Encourage students to use a ruler for accuracy and extend lines beyond the image if necessary.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students build on their understanding of enlargement by using negative scale factors. Begin with scale factors of –2 and –3, with a marked centre of enlargement on a grid. Guide them to count distances from the centre to each vertex, multiplying these distances by the scale factor to locate the corresponding vertices of the image. Explain to students that, unlike positive enlargements, applying a negative scale factor means the distance from the centre of enlargement is measured in the opposite direction. Highlight that a negative scale factor rotates the image 180° while also changing its size. As students develop, encourage them to apply this concept on a coordinate grid, where the centre of enlargement is given as a pair of coordinates. To deepen understanding, ensure students practise enlargements from various centres, including those away from the origin.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students build on their Key Stage 3 understanding of reflection, by reflecting shapes in mirror lines and accurately describing the transformation. Recap reflections in a drawn mirror line, emphasising that the object and image are congruent, and that each vertex is equidistant from the line of reflection. Once students are confident reflecting in drawn lines, introduce reflections defined by an equation. Remind students how to draw the equations of vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines such as y = x or y = –x. For diagonal reflections, model rotating the diagram 45° so that the mirror line becomes vertical or horizontal. Students should also be able to describe a reflection by identifying the line of reflection through corresponding points, finding their midpoints and stating the equation of the line.

Emphasise that translations have no invariant points, as every point moves the same distance and direction, unless the shape remains unchanged.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students interpret velocity–time or speed– time graphs. Ensure that students understand that velocity is a measure of speed in a given direction, whereas speed does not indicate the direction. Students will learn that the gradient at a specific time on a velocity–time graph represents a change in velocity (acceleration). Begin with graphs involving only straight lines, highlighting that positive and negative gradients represent constant acceleration and deceleration, respectively. For curved graphs, model how to draw and calculate the gradient of a tangent at a point, discussing why the accuracy of a tangent may affect answers. Note that students will only look at motion in a single direction, therefore “velocity” and “speed” can be used interchangeably.

small_step_desc: In this small step, students build on their Key Stage 3 understanding of reflection, by reflecting shapes in mirror lines and accurately describing the transformation. Recap reflections in a drawn mirror line, emphasising that the object and image are congruent, and that each vertex is equidistant from the line of reflection. Once students are confident reflecting in drawn lines, introduce reflections defined by an equation. Remind students how to draw the equations of vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines such as y = x or y = –x. For diagonal reflections, model rotating the diagram 45° so that the mirror line becomes vertical or horizontal. Students should also be able to describe a reflection by identifying the line of reflection through corresponding points, finding their midpoints and stating the equation of the line.
